issues.legal_issue: A government grant conferring exclusive possession and substantial rights in land for consideration constitutes a lease when its substance and the parties’ intention show an interest in the property, notwithstanding its description as a licence.
material_facts: The government grant described the grantee as a licensee but permitted it to use the land for a petroleum depot and construct extensive installations.
The grantee had exclusive possession of the land and buildings and carried on its business there without interference.
The grantee paid an annual amount described as rent, and the grant provided for revision of rent and termination on three months’ notice.
The grant restricted assignment and use of the land, but the court found those restrictions were not decisive of the arrangement’s character.
In separate proceedings concerning eviction, the grantee had itself described the arrangement as a tenancy and the payments as rent.
issues.conclusion: The grant constituted a lease, not a licence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2 of the Government Grants Act, 1895, the grant’s terms govern and prevail over inconsistent general rules in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Applying the distinction in Sections 105 of the Transfer of Property Act and 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, the court examines the substance of the document and the parties’ intention: a transfer of an interest in property is a lease, while permission to use property with legal possession remaining with the owner is a licence. Exclusive possession gives rise to a strong but rebuttable presumption of tenancy. The court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Union Bank of India v. Chandrakant Gordhandas Shah, Vayallakath Muhammedkutty v. Illikkal Moosakutty, Om Parkash v. Dr. Ravinder Kumar Sharma, Swarn Singh v. Madan Singh, Lilawati H. Hiranandani v. Usha Tandon, Street v. Mountford, Capt. B. V. D’Souza v. Antonio Fausto Fernandes, and Glenwood Lumber Co. Ltd. v. Philips.

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_appeal and exclusive_possession_granted and extensive_constructions_permitted and (annual_rent_paid or termination_notice_required) and grantee_asserted_tenancy_in_other_proceedings

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: The dispute is an appeal arising from a property-tax assessment of land and installations held under a government grant.
predicates.exclusive_possession_granted: The grant gave the grantee exclusive possession of the land and installations, and the grantee occupied them without interference.
predicates.extensive_constructions_permitted: The grant permitted the grantee to construct extensive buildings and installations for its business.
predicates.annual_rent_paid: The grantee paid an annual amount described in the grant as rent.
predicates.termination_notice_required: The grant required advance notice before either party could terminate it.
predicates.grantee_asserted_tenancy_in_other_procee: In separate proceedings concerning its occupation, the grantee described the arrangement as a tenancy and the payments as rent.

issues.definition: When a property-tax assessment appeal concerns a government grant involving exclusive possession, substantial construction, and terms consistent with rent or a tenancy, the grant creates a lease.

issues.legal_issue: Substantial petroleum storage tanks and associated installations fixed to land for use as a depot are buildings for property-tax purposes.
material_facts: The grantee constructed substantial petroleum storage tanks and associated installations on the land for receiving and storing petroleum products.
The installations formed part of an extensive depot, with an administration block and a boundary wall.
The storage installations had been in place for many years.
issues.conclusion: The petroleum storage tanks are buildings for the purposes of property taxation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(3) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 defines a building to include a structure made of specified or other materials. The court applied that broad definition and relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Indian Oil Corporation, AIR 1991 SC 686, which treated an oil tanker as a building.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: The dispute is an appeal arising from a property-tax assessment concerning land and structures.
predicates.substantial_fixed_storage_tanks_construc: The occupier constructed substantial storage tanks fixed to the land.
predicates.tanks_form_part_of_a_depot: The tanks are used as part of a depot for receiving and storing goods.

issues.definition: When a property-tax assessment appeal concerns substantial storage tanks fixed to land and used as part of a depot, the tanks qualify as buildings for property-tax purposes.

issues.legal_issue: The Union-property tax exemption does not exempt privately owned buildings and installations constructed by a lessee on Union land from property tax assessed on those buildings and installations.
material_facts: The underlying land belonged to the Union, but the buildings and petroleum installations constructed on it belonged to the grantee.
The grantee held the land under a lease and had constructed the installations that were the subject of the composite assessment.
The assessment concerned the constructed installations and the land together, rather than vacant Union land alone.
The grantee’s agreement required it to pay taxes applicable to the land, buildings, tanks, works, and conveniences.
The grantee had occupied and used the constructed installations for many years.
issues.conclusion: The grantee was liable for property tax on the buildings and installations despite the Union’s ownership of the land.
issues.legal_principle: Article 285 of the Constitution and Section 119 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 exempt property of the Union from taxation, but that exemption does not apply to buildings owned by a private grantee merely because they stand on Union land. Sections 114 and 115 concern property taxation, and Section 120(2) places primary liability on a tenant who builds on land let for more than one year. The court distinguished HUDCO v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (2001) 1 SCC 455, which concerned vacant Union land before a lease and construction, and relied on the distinction between that situation and a composite assessment of constructed installations under Section 120(2).

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_appeal and union_owned_land and land_let_to_grantee_as_lessee_for_more_than_one_year and grantee_constructed_and_owns_buildings and assessment_covers_constructed_installations

predicates.property_tax_assessment_appeal: The dispute is an appeal concerning a property-tax assessment of land and structures.
predicates.union_owned_land: The underlying land belongs to the Union.
predicates.land_let_to_grantee_as_lessee_for_more_t: The Union let the land to the grantee as a lessee for a term exceeding one year.
predicates.grantee_constructed_and_owns_buildings: The grantee constructed and owns buildings or installations on the land.
predicates.assessment_covers_constructed_installati: The assessment concerns the constructed buildings or installations, rather than vacant Union land alone.

issues.definition: When a property-tax assessment appeal concerns buildings owned by a grantee who constructed them on Union land let to it for more than one year, the grantee is liable for tax on those constructed buildings or installations.
